newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower, fearing higher rates.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower, fearing higher rates.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended lower on Monday as several factors contributed to the market's fears of higher U.S. interest rates ahead.

"The chief negative seems to be the (December) employment report this Friday," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi. "It's hard to find anyone who has a good thing to say about Friday's employment data -- and that seems to be weighing on us."
Rupkey said the more modest payroll growth estimates are in the neighborhood of 175,000 new jobs.

Wariness on the part of Japanese investors also plagued the market. Japan's markets, closed all last week, reopened on Monday. While some had feared that Tokyo traders would come back to work in a bearish mood, others had hoped that Japanese investors would start the new year as buyers.

"People thought there would be interest from Japan last night and that wasn't the case," said Bill Hornbarger, fixed-income strategist at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "Bond yields have risen by 25 basis points. The thought was if you liked them a week ago at 6-1/2 percent, you gotta love them today at 6-3/4 percent. And that didn't happen."
"There was some concern that Japanese investors did not come in and buy after the holidays," agreed Rupkey.

"The market is just nervous," said Hornbarger. "The economy is coming off what looks like a strong fourth quarter and people are extrapolating from that that the first quarter will be a little stronger than expected and that the Federal Reserve might have to raise interest rates."
Adding to the bond market's jitters were choppy performances by the dollar and the U.S. stock market.
The dollar closed slightly lower after an overnight slump.
The stock market, meanwhile, set another closing high, but only after a roller-coaster day in which stocks first rose sharply, then backtracked and dipped into the minus column.
From a technical point of view, people believe that the market has not finished testing the bottom, said Rupkey.
"There was some talk on Friday that real investors were putting money to work and apparently they were, but that's usually not enough to counter a solid downtrend," Rupkey said.
Rupkey said the the cash bond extended its downtrend on Monday, breaking a low of 96-20/32 reached last Thursday.
The bellwether 30-year U.S. Treasury bond ended at 96-16/32 on Monday, down 16/32, to yield 6.77 percent.
"When you take out the new lows, it's a sign of a weak market," said Rupkey.

Remarks by Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta President Jack Guynn in Atlanta seemed to be neutral for the market. The Atlanta Fed President said he anticipated 1997 U.S. GDP growth of 2-2.5 percent and an increase in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) of three percent.
Rates ended little changed at the short end of the maturity range.
Three-month bill rates were up one basis point to 5.04 percent. Six-month bill rates slipped one basis point to 5.11 percent. Year bill rates ended unchanged at 5.30 percent.
Two-year notes slipped 1/32 to end at 99-19/32, yielding 5.97 percent. Five-year notes fell 3/32 to 99-9/32, yielding 6.29 percent.
Ten-year notes dropped 8/32 to 99-23/32, yielding 6.54 percent.
-- North American Treasury Desk 212-859-1660
